articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
- **Philippines' "assertive transparency" strategy**: Since 2023, the Philippines has deliberately provoked incidents at Renai Jiao (Second Thomas Shoal), documenting and disseminating viral videos of confrontations to frame China as an aggressor and Manila as the victim, with the aim of securing domestic budgetary and equipment support from the Philippine Congress for its coastguard.

- **China's diplomatic focus on rule-making**: Beijing has concentrated its diplomatic capital on institutional frameworks such as Code of Conduct (COC) consultations ongoing since 2013 and the 56th session of DOC working group meetings in Vietnam, rather than engaging in public confrontation.

- **Narrative shift in Beijing's approach**: After initially losing ground in the information war—particularly during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and subsequent incidents at Sabina Shoal—China has adjusted its counter-strategy to proactively expose what it views as Manila's false narratives and smearing tactics.

- **Beijing does not rule out construction at Scarborough Shoal**: The interview suggests China's strategy may shift from reactive defense to proactive action, including potential construction at Scarborough Shoal, as part of a broader paradigm shift driven by lessons learned from countering the Philippines' public relations playbook.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
- **Trump's two-pronged strategy**: Trump's approach centers on (1) consolidating the US sphere of influence in the Western Hemisphere—viewing China and Russia's presence in the region as a national security threat—and (2) "offshore balancing," shifting US focus from global commitments to domestic priorities and the "backyard," effectively transforming the Monroe Doctrine into what Zheng terms the "Donroe Doctrine."

- **Structural disruption from US repositioning**: Zheng argues that the US retreat from post-WWII embedded interests in Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia will create local chaos, while its pivot to Latin America could similarly disrupt regional order, with turbulence likely defining the coming years regardless of whether the US advances or retreats.

- **Three levels of rapid change**: Zheng identifies big-power relations as the primary driver of geopolitical shifts; a US right-wing think tank consensus on a "tripartite partition of the world," with Trump following Putin in pursuing this objective under different pretexts; and the rise of "regional lords" (e.g., Turkey among Turkic-speaking countries) asserting themselves as middle powers.

- **Risk of chain reactions**: Zheng warns that US-Russia compromises—such as ceding Ukrainian territory to end the war—could embolden further aggression, as European states like Poland already fear Ukraine will not be Russia's final target, with Venezuela likely not the last target of US pressure either.

- **China's strategic calculus**: Zheng emphasizes that China does not seek a "separate kitchen" from the existing world order, suggesting China prefers stability within the current framework rather than fragmentation into competing blocs.

articles.summary:
- Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture.
- Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on...

articles.title: Jeffrey Sachs says US sabre-rattling at China can become self-fulfilling prophecy of war
articles.summary:
- **Trade frictions to persist but with limits**: Sachs predicts that neither the US nor China can impose its will on the other, as both hold economic leverage over each other (e.g., China's rare earths). Mutual economic interest will create some restraint, but Trump's unpredictability means agreements will not hold in their details.

- **US started the trade war**: Sachs emphasizes that this is not a mutual dispute but the US attacking China, and warns the US needs to show greater prudence and caution.

- **China should pivot export strategy**: Sachs advises China to focus on growing exports to Africa, Southeast Asia, South Asia, West Asia, Central Asia, and Latin America rather than relying on the US or western European markets, which will remain unfriendly and non-trustworthy.

- **China learned it can push back**: The US was forced to reconsider its tariff posture after China's rare earths countermeasure, signaling that both sides have mutual vulnerabilities that constrain escalation.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
- **Exports to the US are a smaller portion of China's economy than commonly believed**: Exports to the US comprised only about 2.8% of China's GDP, with total exports accounting for roughly 19% of GDP last year. Even a complete loss of the US export market would impact only about 2–3% of China's economy.

- **China's export portfolio has diversified significantly**: Asean is now China's largest export destination (around 16% of total exports), surpassing both the US and EU. Exports to emerging markets grew strongly — 23.3% to Brazil in 2024 and 25.9% to Africa in the first eight months of 2025.

- **The US-China rivalry has expanded beyond trade**: It now extends into technology, ideologies, and global collaboration, and Liu Qian warns that continued unhealthy competition will harm both countries and the world at large.

- **Chinese exporters have shown resilience and adaptability**: Exporters have creatively shifted to new markets, routes, products, and packaging, and exports have generally held steady this year despite tariff pressures.

- **Liu Qian's background and perspective**: As founder of Wusawa Advisory, former managing director of The Economist Group in Greater China, and the only Chinese representative in the core working group of the UN Women Leaders Network, she brings a unique lens on innovation differences between China and the West and advocates for greater women's representation in policymaking.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
• Fuchsia Dunlop is a British author and chef specializing in Chinese cuisine, particularly Sichuanese food, with seven published books, and is regarded as the Western world's most knowledgeable person on China's diverse food cultures.

• Dunlop traveled to China in 1994 as a British Council student at Sichuan University, where she began learning Sichuanese cooking in local restaurants and at the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine, later completing a chef's training course with 50 young Sichuan cooks.

• After returning to England, she discovered no Sichuan cookbooks existed in English despite the region's size rivaling that of a European country, prompting her to conduct research trips back to Sichuan and publish her first Sichuan cookbook in 2001.

• In the interview, Dunlop expressed her fondness for mooncakes, particularly savoury Shanghai minced pork versions and flaky Yunnan ham mooncakes, viewing the Mid-Autumn Festival ritual as another connection with China.

• She notes that Sichuan food has since become highly popular worldwide, and describes writing about Chinese food as a way to continually explore the country's vast cultural and culinary diversity.

articles.title: South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
articles.summary:
- **South Korea's "AI for All" initiative**: President Lee Jae Myung's government is providing every citizen free access to AI, integrating it into hospitals, schools, and government services. A beta launch is set for later this month, offering free, unlimited general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by telecom giants SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao using state-provided Nvidia B200 GPUs.

- **Significant budget commitment**: South Korea has allocated a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, plus an additional 250 billion won for the initiative's rollout through 2027. From next year, the trial is intended to become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility connected to government systems for tasks like booking doctor's appointments and getting tax advice.

- **Risk management framework**: Seoul relies on the AI Basic Act (effective January 2025) to enforce human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments, and synthetic content watermarking. A state-funded AI Safety Institute acts as a technical watchdog, and the government plans an "autonomous reliability-assurance system" based on seven "AI Ethics Principles" including accountability, human-centredness, privacy, and fairness.

- **Contrast with global AI caution**: The article frames South Korea's aggressive AI rollout against warnings from leading AI figures—including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, ex-OpenAI employees, and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton—who have raised concerns about existential risks, autonomous weapons, mass unemployment, deepfakes, and algorithmic bias.

articles.title: US sanctions forced Xinjiang cotton to adapt, but survival comes at a cost
articles.summary:
- **US sanctions impact:** The US UFLPA (2021) imposes a rebuttable presumption that all Xinjiang-produced goods involve forced labour, barring listed companies from exporting to the US unless they provide clear and convincing evidence to the contrary; 187 companies have been blacklisted across sectors as of August additions.

- **Mechanisation surge:** In response to sanctions, Xinjiang has undergone massive agricultural overhaul—over 90% of cotton is now machine-harvested, with satellite-guided seeders, drones, and domestic harvesters pushing mechanisation to nearly 100%; yields have risen to 400kg per mu from 250–300kg under manual labour, and some household incomes have increased 125%.

- **Survival strategies:** Xinjiang's industrial players have adopted a model combining state price supports, rapid mechanisation, technological upgrades, aggressive market diversification, and domestic brand substitution to compensate for loss of US export access.

- **Hidden costs:** On-the-ground sociologists and trade specialists warn that this resilience comes at steep costs, including squeezed profit margins, a chilling effect that has triggered "domestic decoupling" within China, and unintended spillover into European markets.

- **Failed legal remedies:** Targeted companies attempted to fight sanctions through legal channels—e.g., a major yarn spinning giant's Aksu subsidiary was added to the US Commerce Department entity list—though the article notes these efforts largely failed.

articles.title: The myth of brotherhood: Hong Kong’s triads evolve amid new criminal landscape
articles.summary:
• **Triad syndicates are shifting from traditional street violence to white-collar and cybercrime**, including underground banking, cross-border money laundering, and fraud, according to police and anti-triad investigators; the four major remaining syndicates in Hong Kong—Shui Fong, Wo Shing Wo, Sun Yee On, and 14K—have simplified initiation rituals and increasingly operate less as rivals than as profit-driven partners.

• **Triad-related crimes in Hong Kong surged to 2,554 cases in 2022**, a 35% increase from the previous year, driven primarily by a sixfold jump in fraud cases (591 cases, accounting for nearly a quarter of all triad crime that year); between 2016 and 2021, annual cases hovered around 1,700–1,900.

• **The "brotherhood" narrative of triad membership is widely considered a myth**, as described by former member Jason, who found that the organization is fundamentally a profit-making operation where loyalty depends on money rather than solidarity; higher-level members exploit lower-level recruits by outsourcing high-risk tasks to them to minimize personal exposure to arrest.

• **Modern triad crime requires less physical presence**, making it more low-profile and harder to detect, with tasks ranging from property damage to procuring bank accounts for laundering fraudulent funds—often coordinated through messaging apps—representing a fundamental transformation in how syndicates operate and recruit.

articles.title: Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
articles.summary:
• Tesla's Gigafactory in Shanghai is a critical manufacturing hub, producing over half its annual output for export; in July 2023, it delivered 93,579 vehicles, including a record single-shipment of 7,738 units from a Chinese port — creating a potential vulnerability given SpaceX's role as a core US national security contractor.

• Growing technology overlap between Tesla and SpaceX — spanning AI, robotics, batteries, solar panels, satellite internet, and Starlink — has fueled speculation about a possible merger, though Musk has neither confirmed nor denied the idea.

• A merger would create a complex geopolitical dilemma, as Musk would need to balance US national security interests (SpaceX's Pentagon ties) with Tesla's deep reliance on China's supply chain and export market, requiring a ring-fenced strategy acceptable to regulators in both Washington and Beijing.

• Analysts note Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly becoming suppliers to each other, but maintaining this balance is risky given an uncertain geopolitical landscape, according to experts such as Marina Yue Zhang (UTS) and Seth Goldstein (Morningstar).

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
- Tourism accounts for roughly **one-fifth of Thailand's economy**, and visitor numbers have yet to recover to their pre-pandemic peak: nearly **40 million visitors in 2019** vs. **32.9 million in 2024**, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced that year.

- Tourism trends have shifted significantly after Covid-19 — large tour groups (especially from China and Russia) have largely disappeared, replaced by smaller **free, independent tourists (FITs)**, leaving many group-oriented businesses struggling.

- The Tourism Authority of Thailand has **trimmed its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million visitors**, citing rising oil prices from the US-Israel-Iran war and the Ukraine war driving up international airfares, as well as a **strong baht** pushing budget travellers toward cheaper alternatives like Vietnam and Malaysia.

- Beyond economic and geopolitical factors, **rising misbehaviour by foreign tourists** is eroding Thai patience — a growing frustration that is prompting the government to take a harder stance on ill-behaved visitors.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
• **Rising costs are driving Singaporeans away from car ownership**: Certificate of Entitlement (COE) fees have surged dramatically — from S$10,000 in 2006 to over S$112,000 today — while road tax, fuel, maintenance, insurance, and electronic road pricing (ERP) costs continue to climb, prompting residents to reconsider driving.

• **Private car ownership is at a multi-year low**: Land Transport Authority data (July) shows 516,237 privately owned cars on Singapore's roads — the fewest since 2019 — though they still make up 79% of all vehicles. Rental, ride-hailing, and corporate cars have increased in share.

• **Singapore is pushing a "car-lite" strategy**: The LTA's "Move Lite" campaign (launched 2022) promotes walking, cycling, and public transport as sustainable alternatives, shifting messaging to highlight the downsides of driving such as congestion and parking hassles.

• **ERP congestion charges returned to Orchard Road in June 2024**, the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, as part of broader efforts to manage road usage and land scarcity while balancing the needs of all commuters through investment in public transport and active mobility infrastructure.

articles.title: Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
articles.summary:
- **State capital now dominates China's private-equity market**: State-affiliated investors supplied over 90% of committed capital in China's PE market last year, up from just under 79% in 2021 (per Zerone data), as Western dollar funds and domestic private investors retreat amid geopolitical tensions and liquidity mismatch concerns.

- **Capital flows through a multi-layered state-capitalist system**: Public money reaches frontier tech companies like DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics, and CXMT through a complex matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, SOEs, and privately managed funds that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets.

- **Xi Jinping sets explicit investment directives**: At a July 8 national science and technology gathering, Xi urged financial firms to "invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology," signaling that state capital deployment in tech is a direct presidential mandate.

- **Private venture funds increasingly reliant on state money**: Firms like Hangzhou-based Puhua Capital (US$5.91 billion AUM) expect state-affiliated investors to account for ~90% of their 2026 fundraising; the shift began around 2018 when traditional private-business owners pulled back and dollar funds began retreating from China.

- **Outcomes remain uncertain**: The article frames this massive state capital infusion as a make-or-break factor for China's tech self-reliance ambitions, noting that the country's "enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage," raising questions about state-engineered overcapacity.

articles.title: China has dominated tungsten for decades. Can US cash in Central Asia loosen its grip?
articles.summary:
- **China controls roughly 80% of global tungsten mining** (about 3.7 times the output of the rest of the world combined), with dominance extending into processing and manufacturing. Beijing's February 2025 export controls have pushed global tungsten prices up over 200% since May 2025, pressuring US consumers like drill-bit manufacturers, whose production costs have risen as much as 50%.

- **Tungsten demand is driven by defence and technology sectors**, including armour-piercing ammunition, missiles, semiconductors, and AI hardware. The US has had no commercial tungsten mine production since 2015, making overseas supply alternatives strategically critical to Washington.

- **US-backed mining projects are emerging in Kazakhstan**: Cove Capital acquired a 70% stake in two deposits in the Karaganda region (Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty) with a combined estimated development cost of US$1.1 billion, targeting production around 2028.

- **Chinese firms are ahead in the region**: Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources already operates the Boguty Mine commercially in Kazakhstan since April 2025, giving Beijing an established foothold in the same market US projects are trying to enter.

- **Financing alone may not be sufficient**, as analysts note that China's multi-decade industrial system for tungsten — encompassing mining, processing, and manufacturing — cannot be quickly replicated by new market entrants simply by funding new deposits.

articles.title: A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
articles.summary:
• **Envision Group's Galaxy Campus**, a new AI computing facility in Ulanqab, features a 120,000-square-metre data centre designed for up to one million AI accelerators, with a planned power capacity exceeding 2 gigawatts—potentially one of the world's largest AI facilities, surpassing US-based Colossus 2's projected 1.5 GW IT capacity.

• **Ulanqab holds about one-tenth of China's total wind resources** (and one-third of Inner Mongolia's), and roughly 67% of the city's energy comes from green power, including wind and solar, allowing the campus to directly pair computing infrastructure with renewable energy.

• **The city's transformation from a livestock and potato economy to an AI hub followed a decade-long path**, beginning with Huawei's 2013 data centre partnership, followed by Apple's iCloud hosting deal (2018), and subsequent entries by UCloud, Kuaishou, VNET, Centrin Data, and Chindata.

• **As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals**, 86 of which are AI computing projects; AI model start-up DeepSeek was reported to be adding 1 gigawatt of computing capacity to the city.
